brief: Array of n nonzero integers. An operation picks an index i with a_i > 0 and negates the prefix a_1..a_i. Using at most n operations, maximize the final sum and print the operations.
key_idea: Let m be the largest index ever operated: it is hit exactly once, must be originally positive and ends negative; everything after m is untouched and everything before m can be made positive. So answer = max(original sum, max over a_m>0 of sum|a_1..a_{m-1}| - a_m + sum a_{m+1..n}).
solution:
1. Option 0: do nothing (sum of a).
2. For each m with a_m > 0: value = prefAbs(m-1) - a_m + suffixSum(m+1). Take the best m (use long long).
3. Construct for best m: scan i = m-1 down to 1 keeping parity p of ops done; current sign of a_i is sign(a_i) flipped if p=1; if it is positive, operate at i (it becomes negative, p ^= 1). Now a_1..a_{m-1} are all negative.
4. Operate at m (a_m is untouched, still positive): prefix becomes all positive, a_m negative.
5. Total ops <= m <= n. If doing nothing is best print 0.

brief: n x m grid of 0/1. q times a cell is toggled; after each toggle print the maximum, over all rows, of the longest run of consecutive 1s in that row.
key_idea: Cache best run per row; a toggle only changes one row, so recompute that row in O(m) and take max over n rows.
solution:
1. Read grid; best[r] = longest run of 1s in row r (scan keeping current run length cur = a? cur+1 : 0).
2. For each query (i,j): flip g[i][j], recompute best[i] in O(m).
3. Answer = max of best[0..n-1] in O(n).
4. Total O(q(n+m)) = 5000*1000, fine.

brief: Given n and k (2k <= n), print a permutation of 1..2n such that sum |a_{2i-1}-a_{2i}| - |sum (a_{2i-1}-a_{2i})| = 2k.
key_idea: Use pairs (2i-1,2i): each pair contributes |diff|=1. Reverse the first k pairs so their signed difference is +1, the rest -1: value = n - |k-(n-k)| = n-(n-2k) = 2k.
solution:
1. For i = 1..n: if i <= k print 2i, 2i-1; else print 2i-1, 2i.
2. Sum of |differences| = n.
3. Signed sum = k*(+1) + (n-k)*(-1) = 2k-n <= 0, abs = n-2k.
4. Expression = n-(n-2k) = 2k. k=0 just prints 1..2n.

brief: Given a string of upper/lowercase letters (length <= 1e5), change the case of the fewest letters so all uppercase letters come before all lowercase letters.
key_idea: Try every split point s: cost = lowercase letters in [0,s) + uppercase letters in [s,n); take the minimum.
solution:
1. upTotal = number of uppercase letters; cost at s=0 is upTotal.
2. Sweep s from 0 to n-1: if s[i] is lowercase, lowBefore++; else upAfter--.
3. After each step cost = lowBefore + upAfter; keep minimum.
4. Equivalent DP: dp_up/dp_low state machine.

brief: Need n planks of length 18, n of 21 and n of 25; standard planks have length 60 and can be cut but not joined. Find the minimum number of 60-planks (n <= 1000).
key_idea: A plank holding a 25 fits at most 2 pieces (25+18+18=61>60); others fit 3 pieces only as 18+18+18, 18+18+21 or 18+21+21. Lower bound and construction both give ceil(7n/6).
solution:
1. Pieces with 25: pair them, ceil(n/2) planks (a leftover 25 can share with an 18 or 21).
2. 18s and 21s: n/2 planks of (18,21,21) and the rest as (18,18,18) -> 2n/3 planks.
3. Bound: 3n pieces <= 3*P - (#planks with a 25) and that count >= n/2, so P >= 7n/6.
4. Answer = (7n+5)/6 (integer ceil).

#include <bits/stdc++.h>
int main(){long long n;scanf("%lld",&n);printf("%lld\n",(7*n+5)/6);}

brief: Given a permutation a of 1..n, you may swap a_i and a_{i+2} any number of times. Can a become a hill (strictly increasing then strictly decreasing)?
key_idea: Each value keeps its position parity and can be placed anywhere of that parity. A hill is built by placing n, n-1, ... outward from the peak, so every even-length top set occupies a contiguous block with equal odd/even counts: values (n,n-1), (n-2,n-3), ... must each have different parities.
solution:
1. cls[v] = parity of the position where v currently sits.
2. Values in decreasing order fill a growing contiguous interval; an interval of even length has exactly half odd positions.
3. So for j = 0,2,4,... with j+1 < n: cls[n-j] must differ from cls[n-j-1]; otherwise NO.
4. If all pairs differ, a valid placement always exists -> YES (a leftover single value when n is odd is fine).

brief: Multiset of n values (each <= n). One operation: pick x>1 and prime p | x, replace x with p copies of x/p. Find the minimum operations so all elements are <= k.
key_idea: Elements are independent: cost(x) = 0 if x <= k, else min over prime p | x of 1 + p*cost(x/p). Compute bottom-up for x = 1..n with a smallest-prime-factor sieve.
solution:
1. Sieve spf up to 2e5 once.
2. Per test: for x = 1..n: if x <= k cost=0; else iterate distinct primes p of x (via spf) and take min(1 + p*cost[x/p]).
3. Answer = sum of cost[a_i] (long long; can reach ~4e10).
4. x/p < x so cost[x/p] is already computed.
complexity: O(n log n) per test, O(n) space

brief: Split a string (length <= 200) into exactly k consecutive lines, each of length between a and b; print any split or 'No solution'.
key_idea: Feasible iff k*a <= len <= k*b; then give each line a characters and distribute the extra len-k*a greedily (up to b-a per line).
solution:
1. n = |s|. If n < k*a or n > k*b print 'No solution'.
2. extra = n - k*a.
3. For each of k lines: len = a + min(extra, b-a); extra -= that; print next len characters.
4. (DP alternative: can[i][j] = first i chars into j lines.)

brief: n trees ('spiders'), each given by its edges. You may glue beads of different trees together into one tree; maximize the diameter of the result.
key_idea: Glue the end of one tree's diameter to the start of the next: the answer is simply the sum of the diameters of all trees.
solution:
1. For each tree compute its diameter with two BFS/DFS: farthest node u from any node, then farthest distance from u.
2. (Or tree DP: longest two child depths at each node.)
3. Sum diameters.
4. Note: this old round reads from input.txt and writes output.txt (freopen) - check the statement on submission.

brief: n messages; message i may link to earlier message a_i (0 = none). Opening x shows messages x-k..x+k; starting at t you read visible messages and follow links repeatedly. For every t print the number of distinct messages read.
key_idea: Links point backwards, so dp[i] = dp[a_i] + |window(i)| - |window(i) ∩ window(a_i)|; the overlap is [L_i, R_{a_i}] since everything the chain from a_i reads lies at or left of R_{a_i}.
solution:
1. L_i = max(1,i-k), R_i = min(n,i+k).
2. If a_i = 0: dp[i] = R_i - L_i + 1.
3. Else j=a_i: dp[i] = dp[j] + (R_i-L_i+1) - max(0, R_j - L_i + 1).
4. Process i increasing (j < i). Print dp.

brief: A list of file names 'name.ext' (name 1-8 lowercase letters, ext 1-3) was concatenated without separators (string up to 4e5 of letters and dots). Split it back into valid names or print NO.
key_idea: ok[i] = prefix of length i can be split; a valid piece has length 3..12 and exactly one dot with 1-8 letters before and 1-3 after. Store a parent pointer to rebuild.
solution:
1. ok[0]=true. For i = 1..n and len = 3..12 (len <= i): if ok[i-len] and s[i-len, i) is a valid name, set ok[i]=true, par[i]=i-len, break.
2. Valid piece: exactly one '.', its position p satisfies 1 <= p <= 8 and 1 <= len-p-1 <= 3.
3. If !ok[n] print NO.
4. Otherwise follow par from n back to 0, reverse the cut list, print YES and the pieces.
5. (A greedy over dots also works, DP is safer.)

brief: Given n numbers (values up to 1e5), repeatedly pick a value v, gain v points, and delete all elements equal to v-1 and v+1 (picking v again is allowed). Maximize total points.
key_idea: Group by value: taking value v means taking all copies (v*cnt[v]) and forbidding v-1, v+1 -> house-robber DP over values.
solution:
1. cnt[v] = frequency.
2. dp[0]=0, dp[1]=cnt[1].
3. dp[v] = max(dp[v-1], dp[v-2] + v*cnt[v]) for v = 2..1e5.
4. Answer dp[maxV]; use long long (up to 1e10).

brief: Given an uppercase string (length <= 1e5), decide whether it contains non-overlapping substrings 'AB' and 'BA' (any order).
key_idea: Take the first occurrence of one pattern and look for the other only from 2 positions after it; try both orders.
solution:
1. i = s.find("AB"); if found and s.find("BA", i+2) != npos -> YES.
2. j = s.find("BA"); if found and s.find("AB", j+2) != npos -> YES.
3. Otherwise NO.
4. Earliest first occurrence is optimal because it leaves the longest suffix for the second.

brief: n trees at sorted distinct positions x_i with heights h_i. Each tree can be felled left [x-h,x], right [x,x+h], or left standing; segments may not contain any occupied point. Maximize felled trees.
key_idea: Scan left to right: prefer felling left (uses no future space), else fell right if it does not reach the next tree, else leave it; track the last occupied coordinate.
solution:
1. last = -inf, ans = 0.
2. For tree i: if x_i - h_i > last: fell left, ans++, last = x_i.
3. Else if i is the last tree or x_i + h_i < x_{i+1}: fell right, ans++, last = x_i + h_i.
4. Else last = x_i (stands).
5. Use long long for x+h. (DP with states left/stand/right gives the same.)

brief: Given a number with up to 100 digits, delete some digits (keeping order) so the remaining non-empty number has no leading zeros and is divisible by 8; print YES and it, or NO.
key_idea: Divisibility by 8 depends only on the last three digits (1000 % 8 == 0), so some 1-, 2- or 3-digit subsequence works whenever any answer does.
solution:
1. Try every single digit: 0 or 8 -> answer.
2. Try every pair i<j: 10*d_i+d_j divisible by 8 (d_i != 0) -> answer.
3. Try every triple i<j<k: 100*d_i+10*d_j+d_k divisible by 8 (d_i != 0).
4. If none: NO. A longer valid answer ends in a valid <=3-digit tail, and if that tail has a leading zero the single digit 0 exists.

brief: n bosses, each easy(0) or hard(1). Friend and you alternate turns (friend first), each turn killing 1 or 2 next bosses. Each hard boss killed by the friend costs a skip point. Minimize skip points.
key_idea: dp[i][who] = min skips to kill bosses i..n-1 when it is who's turn; each turn take 1 or 2 bosses.
solution:
1. dp[n][*] = 0 (also allow overshoot: taking 2 needs i+2 <= n).
2. Friend's turn: dp[i][0] = min(a_i + dp[i+1][1], a_i + a_{i+1} + dp[i+2][1]).
3. Your turn: dp[i][1] = min(dp[i+1][0], dp[i+2][0]).
4. Answer dp[0][0]. Fill i from n-1 down.

brief: n potions (n <= 2000) with health changes a_i (possibly negative). Walking left to right from 0 health, choose which to drink so health never becomes negative; maximize the number drunk.
key_idea: Drink every potion; if health goes negative, undo the most negative potion drunk so far (min-heap). Alternative DP: dp[j] = max health after drinking j potions.
solution:
1. health = 0, min-heap of drunk values.
2. For each a_i: drink it (health += a_i, push a_i).
3. If health < 0: pop the smallest value v, health -= v.
4. Answer = heap size. Use long long.
5. Exchange argument: dropping the most negative potion keeps the count and maximizes health.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

brief: Array of n (<= 2000) numbers; repeatedly replace two adjacent elements by their XOR. Can you end with at least 2 elements, all equal?
key_idea: Final pieces are XORs of contiguous segments. If total XOR is 0, split into 2 parts (YES). Otherwise you need >= 3 segments each with XOR = total.
solution:
1. X = XOR of all elements. If X == 0 -> YES (any prefix and its complement are equal).
2. Else greedily scan: cur ^= a_i; when cur == X, cnt++, cur = 0.
3. If cnt >= 3 -> YES (extra segments merge in pairs/with leftover xor 0), else NO.
4. An odd count of X-segments is required; 3 suffices.

brief: An ant on a tetrahedron ABCD starts at D and moves along an edge each step. Count walks of exactly n steps (n <= 1e7) that end at D, modulo 1e9+7.
key_idea: Two states: d = ways to be at D, o = ways to be at one particular other vertex. d' = 3o, o' = d + 2o.
solution:
1. d = 1, o = 0 at step 0.
2. Repeat n times: nd = 3*o mod p; no = (d + 2*o) mod p.
3. Answer d after n steps.
4. O(1) memory (n up to 1e7). Closed form also exists: (3^n + 3*(-1)^n)/4.

brief: A sequence is beautiful if it splits into blocks where each block starts with a number equal to the count of elements after it in that block. Find the minimum deletions to make a given sequence (n <= 2e5) beautiful.
key_idea: dp[i] = min deletions for suffix starting at i: either delete a_i, or start a block at i that covers exactly the next a_i elements.
solution:
1. dp[n] = 0.
2. For i = n-1 down to 0: dp[i] = dp[i+1] + 1 (delete a_i).
3. If i + a_i + 1 <= n: dp[i] = min(dp[i], dp[i + a_i + 1]).
4. Answer dp[0].

brief: String of 'a'/'b' of length n (<= 1e5); you may change at most k characters. Maximize the length of the longest block of equal letters.
key_idea: For each target letter c, find the longest window containing at most k letters different from c (sliding window).
solution:
1. For c in {'a','b'}: l = 0, bad = 0.
2. For r = 0..n-1: if s[r] != c, bad++.
3. While bad > k: if s[l] != c, bad--; l++.
4. best = max(best, r-l+1).
5. Answer best over both letters.

brief: Array a and binary string s (n, q <= 1e5). Queries: '1 l r' flips s_l..s_r; '2 g' prints XOR of all a_i with s_i = g (0 if none).
key_idea: Keep X0 and X1 (XOR of a_i with s_i = 0 / 1). Flipping [l,r] moves every element of the range to the other group, which is just X0 ^= seg, X1 ^= seg where seg = prefix-XOR of the range.
solution:
1. P[i] = a_1 ^ ... ^ a_i.
2. X1 = XOR of a_i with s_i='1', X0 = XOR with '0'.
3. Query 1 l r: seg = P[r] ^ P[l-1]; X0 ^= seg; X1 ^= seg.
4. Query 2 g: print g ? X1 : X0.
5. Print answers of each test on one line.

brief: Starting from l, add 1 repeatedly until reaching r (1 <= l < r <= 1e9); each addition changes some trailing digits. Output the total number of changed digits.
key_idea: Counting from 0 to x, the k-th digit (from the right) changes floor(x/10^k) times, so f(x) = sum_k floor(x/10^k) and the answer is f(r) - f(l).
solution:
1. f(x): s = 0; while x > 0: s += x; x /= 10.
2. Answer = f(r) - f(l).
3. Use long long (about 1.1e9).
complexity: O(log r) per test, O(1) space

brief: String of length n = 2^k. A string is c-good if it is the single char c, or one half is all c and the other half is (c+1)-good. Find the minimum single-character changes to make s 'a'-good.
key_idea: Divide and conquer: cost(l,r,c) = min(nonC(left) + cost(right,c+1), nonC(right) + cost(left,c+1)).
solution:
1. solve(l, r, c): if r - l == 1 return s[l] != c.
2. mid = (l+r)/2; count chars != c in each half (O(len)).
3. Return min(cntL + solve(mid,r,c+1), cntR + solve(l,mid,c+1)).
4. Each level costs O(n), log n levels.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(log n) stack

brief: Tree with n cities (n <= 1e5). Starting at city 1, a horse repeatedly moves to a uniformly random unvisited neighbour until none remains. Output the expected journey length.
key_idea: Rooted at 1, unvisited neighbours are exactly the children; E(v) = average over children c of (1 + E(c)), E(leaf) = 0.
solution:
1. Root the tree at 1; iterative DFS to get parent and order.
2. Process nodes in reverse order: E(v) = sum(1 + E(c)) / (#children), 0 if none.
3. Print E(1) with enough precision.
4. Equivalent: sum over leaves of depth * probability of reaching it.

brief: A number is powerful if it is a power of two or a factorial. Given n <= 1e12, find the minimum number of DISTINCT powerful numbers summing to n (or -1).
key_idea: Only factorials 3!..14! (12 of them) are not powers of two; brute-force every subset of them, and cover the remainder with its binary representation (popcount).
solution:
1. Precompute f = {6, 24, ..., 14!} (12 values; 15! > 1e12; 1!,2! are powers of two).
2. For each mask of 4096 subsets: S = sum; if S <= n, candidate = popcount(mask) + popcount(n - S).
3. Answer = min candidate (always exists, so never -1).
4. Distinctness holds: binary bits are distinct powers of two, and none equals a chosen factorial >= 6.

brief: A string is good if its left and right cyclic shifts are equal. Given a digit string (length <= 2e5), erase the minimum number of characters to make it good.
key_idea: Good strings are either one repeated digit or an even-length alternation abab...; try all 100 digit pairs (a,b) and greedily take the longest alternating subsequence.
solution:
1. For each pair (a, b) of digits: walk s, expecting a then b then a ...; take a char when it equals the expected one, flip expectation.
2. If a != b and the taken length is odd, subtract 1.
3. If a == b the count is just the occurrences of a (any length ok).
4. Answer = n - max length.

brief: Given an array (n <= 2e5), remove at most one element to maximize the length of a strictly increasing contiguous subarray.
key_idea: L[i] = increasing run ending at i, R[i] = increasing run starting at i; removing i joins L[i-1] and R[i+1] when a[i-1] < a[i+1].

brief: Count the multisets of positive palindromic integers that sum to n (n <= 4e4, t <= 1e4 queries), modulo 1e9+7.
key_idea: Unbounded-knapsack counting over the ~500 palindromes below 4e4 (coins loop outer so order does not matter); precompute once for all queries.
solution:
1. Collect all palindromes p <= 40000.
2. dp[0] = 1.
3. For each p (outer loop), for s = p..40000: dp[s] = (dp[s] + dp[s-p]) % MOD.
4. Answer each query with dp[n].
complexity: O(P * N) ≈ 2e7 precompute, O(1) per query, O(N) space

brief: An AC starts at temperature m at time 0 and can change temperature by -1, 0 or +1 per minute. n customers (sorted by time t_i) each want the temperature in [l_i, h_i] at time t_i. Can all be satisfied?
key_idea: Track the interval [lo, hi] of reachable temperatures: after dt minutes it widens by dt on each side, then intersect with the customer's range.
solution:
1. lo = hi = m, prev = 0.
2. For each customer: dt = t - prev; lo -= dt; hi += dt.
3. lo = max(lo, l), hi = min(hi, h). If lo > hi -> NO.
4. prev = t. If all pass -> YES. Use long long.

brief: Array of n positive integers (n, a_i <= 5000). One operation: choose i != j and set a_i = gcd(a_i, a_j). Find the minimum operations to make all elements equal.
key_idea: Everything must become g = gcd(all). If some a_i = g, each other element needs 1 op. Otherwise first build g in one element using the smallest subset with gcd g (k elements -> k-1 ops), then n-1 more ops.
solution:
1. g = gcd of all; cnt = number of a_i == g. If cnt > 0 answer n - cnt.
2. Else divide all by g (target becomes 1). dp[v] = min #elements whose gcd is v (values <= 5000), INF initially.
3. For each a: for every v with dp[v] < INF: dp[gcd(v,a)] = min(dp[gcd(v,a)], dp[v]+1); also dp[a] = 1.
4. Answer = (dp[1] - 1) + (n - 1).
complexity: O(n * V * log V) with V = 5000, O(V) space

brief: Strings s (n) and t (m), t is a subsequence of s. Choose positions p_1<...<p_m matching t; maximize max(p_{i+1} - p_i).
key_idea: L[i] = earliest position matching t[i] in a leftmost greedy match, R[i] = latest position in a rightmost greedy match; answer = max over i of R[i+1] - L[i].
solution:
1. Greedy from left: j over s, for i = 0..m-1 advance until s[j] == t[i]; L[i] = j.
2. Greedy from right similarly: R[i] = latest valid position.
3. Answer = max_{i<m-1} (R[i+1] - L[i]).
4. Valid because L[0..i] and R[i+1..] can be combined (L[i] < R[i+1]).

brief: n balls in a row with colors. Operation: choose i<j with equal colors and remove balls i..j. Maximize the total number of removed balls.
key_idea: dp[i] = max removed among the first i balls; ball i is kept (dp[i-1]) or ends a removed segment starting at an earlier j of the same color: dp[j-1] + (i-j+1). Keep best[c] = max(dp[j-1] - j + 1) per color.
solution:
1. dp[0] = 0, best[c] = -INF.
2. For i = 1..n with color c: dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], i + best[c]).
3. Then best[c] = max(best[c], dp[i-1] - i + 1) (ball i as a future left end).
4. Answer dp[n].

brief: Given a tree with n vertices (n <= 1e5), remove the maximum number of edges so that every component has an even number of vertices; print -1 if impossible.
key_idea: If n is odd it's impossible. Otherwise an edge (v, parent) can be cut exactly when subtree size of v is even; count such v.
solution:
1. If n is odd print -1.
2. Root at 1, compute subtree sizes (iterative DFS + reverse order).
3. Answer = number of non-root vertices with even subtree size.
4. Cuts are independent: each piece then has even size.
dry_run:
Sample 1: edges 2-4, 4-1, 3-1; root 1.
size(2)=1, size(4)=2, size(3)=1.
Even non-root sizes: vertex 4 -> answer 1.
Sample 2 (n=3) -> -1.

brief: Given n, k and a string s over the first k letters, decide whether every length-n string over those letters is a subsequence of s; if not, output one that is not.
key_idea: Greedily cut s into blocks that each contain all k letters; the letter that completes a block is the worst choice for an adversary. If fewer than n blocks, the completing letters + a letter missing from the leftover part form a non-subsequence.
solution:
1. Scan s with a set of seen letters; when its size reaches k, record the current char, count++, clear the set.
2. If count >= n print YES.
3. Else build ans = recorded chars (count of them) + any letter among first k not in the current partial set.
4. Pad with 'a' up to length n. Print NO and ans.
complexity: O(m + n) per test, O(k) space
dry_run:
Sample n=2,k=2,s=abb: 'a','b' -> block done at 'b', count=1; leftover {'b'}.
count 1 < 2 -> ans = 'b' + missing 'a' = 'ba'.
'ba' is not a subsequence of abb -> NO ba (sample prints aa; any valid accepted).

brief: Strip of n cells with k air conditioners at positions a_j with temperatures t_j. For each cell i output min_j (t_j + |a_j - i|).
key_idea: Two sweeps: left-to-right carries best = min(best+1, own t), right-to-left the same; answer is the min of both.
solution:
1. c[i] = t_j if a conditioner is at i, else INF.
2. L[i] = min(c[i], L[i-1] + 1) for i = 1..n.
3. R[i] = min(c[i], R[i+1] + 1) for i = n..1.
4. Answer min(L[i], R[i]). Use long long; input has blank lines (scanf skips them).

brief: Rooted tree (root 1) with values a_i >= 0. Operation on a vertex v with children: a_v += 1 and every other vertex in v's subtree -= 1; values must stay non-negative. Maximize a_1.
key_idea: Compute f(v) = the largest value m such that every vertex in v's subtree can be kept >= m when the parent pulls; leaf: a_v; internal: m = min child f; if a_v >= m then f = m else f = (a_v + m) / 2. Root answer = a_1 + min child f.
solution:
1. Build children lists from parents; get BFS order from root and process in reverse.
2. Leaf: f = a_v.
3. Internal non-root: m = min f(child); f = a_v >= m ? m : (a_v + m) / 2 (raise a_v by operating on v, which lowers the subtree equally).
4. Root: answer = a_1 + min f(child).
5. Use long long. (Binary search on answer also works.)

brief: String of 'D' and 'K' (n <= 5e5). For every prefix, output the maximum number of pieces it can be cut into so all pieces have the same D:K ratio.
key_idea: All pieces must share the prefix's own ratio; the answer for prefix i is the number of earlier prefixes (including itself) with the same reduced ratio (d/g, k/g).
solution:
1. Keep counts d, k of the current prefix.
2. g = gcd(d, k); key = (d/g, k/g).
3. cnt[key]++ and output cnt[key].
4. Each earlier prefix with the same ratio is a valid cut point, and they are exactly the cut points.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run:
Own example: DDK.
'D' -> (1,0) cnt 1 -> 1. 'DD' -> (1,0) cnt 2 -> 2.
'DDK' -> (2,1) cnt 1 -> 1. Output 1 2 1.

brief: Capital at 0, kingdoms at x_1<...<x_n. Moving the capital to a conquered kingdom costs a per unit; conquering costs b per unit distance from the capital (no unconquered kingdom in between). Minimize total cost.
key_idea: Optimal strategy: conquer kingdoms in order, moving the capital along up to some final kingdom i, then conquer the rest from x_i. Cost(i) = (a+b)*x_i + b*(sum_{j>i} x_j - (n-i)*x_i); try all i (x_0 = 0).
solution:
1. suffix = sum of all x.
2. For i = 0..n (x_0 = 0): when i >= 1 subtract x_i from suffix.
3. cost = (a+b)*x_i + b*(suffix - (n-i)*x_i).
4. Answer = min cost. Use long long (values up to ~2e5 * 1e8 * 1e5 needs care: ~2e18 fits).

brief: For a permutation, connect each index to the nearest larger element on its left and on its right. Count permutations of length n (n <= 1e6) whose graph has a cycle, mod 1e9+7.
key_idea: Acyclic permutations are exactly the unimodal ones (increase then decrease), and there are 2^(n-1) of them (each value except n goes left or right of the peak). Answer = n! - 2^(n-1).
solution:
1. fact = n! mod p.
2. pw = 2^(n-1) mod p.
3. Answer = (fact - pw + p) % p.
4. A cycle appears iff some element has larger neighbours on both sides (a 'valley').
dry_run:
Sample n=4: 4! = 24.
2^3 = 8 unimodal permutations.
24 - 8 = 16 (expected 16).

brief: n sweets with sugar a_i; at most m sweets per day, eating sweet i on day d costs d*a_i. For every k = 1..n output the minimum cost of eating exactly k sweets.
key_idea: Take the k smallest; the largest m go on day 1, the next m on day 2, ... Hence x_k = x_{k-m} + (sum of the k smallest).
solution:
1. Sort a ascending; S_k = prefix sum.
2. x_k = S_k + (k > m ? x_{k-m} : 0).
3. Reason: moving from k-m to k pushes every previously eaten sweet one day later (adds S_{k-m}) and adds the m new ones on day 1; total = S_k + x_{k-m}.
4. Use long long.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

brief: Array of values in {1,2,3} (n <= 2e5). A subsequence is beautiful if length >= 3, every element except the first has a smaller element to its left, and every element except the last has a larger one to its right. Count beautiful subsequences mod 998244353.
key_idea: With values 1..3 a beautiful subsequence is exactly 1, then one or more 2s, then 3. Count with a small state DP.
solution:
1. c1 = number of 1s seen; d = number of subsequences '1 2+' seen so far.
2. On 1: c1++.
3. On 2: d = 2*d + c1 (extend every existing one or not, or start a new one after any 1).
4. On 3: ans += d.
5. All mod 998244353.

brief: Array of n (<= 2000) integers; one operation replaces one of two adjacent elements by their gcd. Find the minimum operations to make all elements 1, or -1.
key_idea: If there are c ones already, answer n - c. Otherwise find the shortest subarray with gcd 1 (length L): L-1 ops create one 1, then n-1 ops spread it.
solution:
1. Count ones c; if c > 0 print n - c.
2. For each start i, extend j with running gcd until it becomes 1; track min length L = j-i+1.
3. If no subarray has gcd 1 print -1.
4. Else print (L-1) + (n-1).
complexity: O(n^2 log A) time, O(1) space

brief: Cards 1..n are laid out in phases: odd numbers, then 2*odd, 3*odd, 4*odd, ... (only unplaced cards, increasing). Output the k-th card placed (n, k <= 1e9).
key_idea: Only phases with multiplier a power of two place new cards: phase 2^j places cards 2^j * odd, and there are (n/2^j + 1)/2 of them.
solution:
1. j = 1 (multiplier).
2. c = (n/j + 1)/2 = number of odd m with j*m <= n.
3. If k <= c answer j*(2k-1); else k -= c, j *= 2.
4. Loop at most ~30 times.
complexity: O(log n) per test, O(1) space

brief: l <= r with the same number of digits (< 1e9). f(a,b) = number of positions where a and b have equal digits. Minimize f(l,x) + f(x,r) over l <= x <= r.
key_idea: Shared prefix digits of l and r are forced (cost 2 each). At the first differing position: gap >= 2 lets x pick a middle digit and be free afterwards; gap 1 costs 1, plus 1 for each following position where l has 9 and r has 0.
solution:
1. p = length of common prefix; ans = 2p. If p == len, answer 2*len.
2. If r[p] - l[p] >= 2: answer ans.
3. Else ans += 1 (x takes l[p] or r[p]).
4. For i = p+1.. while l[i]=='9' and r[i]=='0': ans += 1 (x must copy one of them to stay in range); stop at first other position.
5. Print ans.

brief: n buttons with weights a_i. Clones can be created at any button and walk left/right, pressing unpressed buttons they land on. All buttons must be pressed in non-increasing weight order. Minimize clones created.
key_idea: After merging equal adjacent values, every local maximum (strictly larger than both neighbours) needs its own clone, and one clone per peak suffices.
solution:
1. Compress consecutive equal values into b.
2. Count i where (i == 0 or b[i] > b[i-1]) and (i == last or b[i] > b[i+1]).
3. That count is the answer.
4. A clone at a peak can walk down both slopes; a peak can't be reached from a lower pressed button in order.
dry_run:
Sample 1 7 9 7 1 10 2 10 10 7 -> compressed 1 7 9 7 1 10 2 10 7.
Peaks: 9, 10 (pos 5), 10 (pos 7).
Answer 3 (expected 3).

brief: Type string s left to right; for each character either type it or press Backspace (deletes the last typed char). Can the final text be exactly t?
key_idea: Match from the end: if s[i] == t[j] take it; otherwise s[i] is unwanted: press Backspace instead of typing it, which also erases one earlier typed char, so skip two characters of s.
solution:
1. i = |s|-1, j = |t|-1.
2. While i >= 0 and j >= 0: if s[i] == t[j]: i--, j--; else i -= 2.
3. YES iff j < 0 (any leftover prefix of s can be wiped: backspace on empty text does nothing).
4. Greedy from the end is optimal because the last kept char must match t's last char.
dry_run:
Sample s=ababa, t=ba: i=4 'a'=t[1] -> i3,j0.
s[3]='b'=t[0] -> j=-1 -> YES.
Sample s=ababa,t=bb: 'a'!='b' skip2 -> i=2 'a' skip -> i=0 'a' skip -> NO.

brief: c was formed by interleaving strings a and b (keeping each one's order), then some characters of c were changed. Find the minimum number of changed characters.
key_idea: dp[i][j] = min mismatches when the first i chars of a and first j of b form the first i+j chars of c.
dry_run:
Sample a=ab, b=cd, c=acbd: path a(a) c(c) b(b) d(d) has 0 mismatches.
dp[1][0]=0, dp[1][1]=0, dp[2][1]=0, dp[2][2]=0.
Answer 0.

brief: The sequence of positive integers that do not contain the digit 4: 1,2,3,5,6,... Output the k-th element (k <= 1e12).
key_idea: Numbers without digit 4 are base-9 numbers with digits 0..8 mapped to 0,1,2,3,5,6,7,8,9: write k in base 9 and map digits >= 4 to digit+1.
solution:
1. Convert k to base 9 (least significant first).
2. Map each digit d -> d < 4 ? d : d+1.
3. Read digits from most significant to build the answer (long long).
4. Works because the k-th valid number corresponds to the base-9 representation of k.
complexity: O(log k) per test, O(1) space

brief: Array a (n <= 3e5, a_i <= 1e12). Operation: choose 1 < i <= |a| with a_i = |a| + 1 - i, then append i-1 zeros. Maximize the final length.
key_idea: Index i (original, since zeros never qualify) is usable exactly when the current length is u_i = a_i + i - 1, and moves the length to u_i + i - 1. Build a graph on lengths and find the largest length reachable from n.
solution:
1. For each i in 2..n: u = a_i + i - 1, v = u + i - 1; add edge u -> v (map<long long, vector>).
2. BFS/DFS from length n with a visited set.
3. Answer = max visited length.
4. Appended zeros never satisfy a_i = |a|+1-i >= 1... (they are 0), so only original indices matter.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run:
Sample a=2 4 6 2 5 (n=5): edges i2: 5->6, i3: 8->10, i4: 5->8, i5: 9->13.
From 5: reach 6, 8; from 8 reach 10.
Max 10 (expected 10).

brief: A string is alternating if its length is even, all odd positions hold one letter and all even positions hold one letter. Using at most one deletion and any number of replacements, minimize operations to make s alternating.
key_idea: Even n: no deletion; cost = (n/2 - max freq on even positions) + (n/2 - max freq on odd positions). Odd n: must delete one char; try every i using prefix counts per parity and suffix counts per parity (suffix parities swap after deletion).
solution:
1. If n even: cnt[p][c] over parity p; answer n - max_c cnt[0][c] - max_c cnt[1][c].
2. If n odd: suf[p][c] = counts over the whole string initially; pre[p][c] = 0.
3. For i = 0..n-1: remove s[i] from suf; new even counts = pre[0] + suf[1], new odd = pre[1] + suf[0]; cost = 1 + (n-1) - maxEven - maxOdd; then add s[i] to pre[i%2].
4. Answer min cost (n=1 gives 1).
dry_run:
Sample 'ababa' (n=5): delete i=0 -> 'baba': even b x2, odd a x2.
cost = 1 + 4 - 2 - 2 = 1.
Sample 'ca' (even): max 1 + 1 -> 2-2 = 0.

brief: n potion types with buy costs c_i; k types are free. Each potion has at most one recipe (list of other potions, acyclic). For every potion output the minimum cost to obtain it.
key_idea: cost(i) = 0 if free, else min(c_i, sum of cost(ingredients)) when a recipe exists; memoized DFS on the DAG.
solution:
1. Set c_i = 0 for free potions.
2. Memoized DFS: cost(i) = c_i if no recipe, else min(c_i, sum cost(j) for j in recipe).
3. Use an explicit stack (post-order) to avoid deep recursion on 2e5 nodes.
4. Use long long (sums up to 2e5 * 1e9).
complexity: O(n + sum m_i) time, O(n) space
dry_run:
Own example: n=3, c=[5,10,3], free {3}; recipe(1) = {2,3}.
cost3 = 0, cost2 = 10.
cost1 = min(5, 10+0) = 5. Output 5 10 0.

brief: Two rows of n pipes; types 1-2 are straight and 3-6 curved, and any pipe can be rotated. Water enters left of (1,1) and must exit right of (2,n). Answer YES/NO per query.
key_idea: After rotation only 'straight' vs 'curved' matters. Walk column by column: straight keeps the row; curved forces a switch, which needs the other row's pipe in that column to be curved too.
solution:
1. r = 0 (top row).
2. For column i: if pipe[r][i] <= 2, continue in row r.
3. Else if pipe[1-r][i] >= 3: r = 1-r (go through both curved pipes); else fail.
4. YES iff no failure and r == 1 at the end.
dry_run:
Sample n=2, rows '13','24': col0 top '1' straight -> r=0.
col1 top '3' curved, bottom '4' curved -> r=1.
End r=1 -> YES.
Sample '12','34': col1 top '2' straight, end r=0 -> NO.

brief: Benches 1..n, m cookie sellers at given benches. Walking from 1 to n, Petya eats at bench i if a seller is there, or it is his first cookie, or d minutes passed since the last one. Remove exactly one seller to minimize cookies; print the minimum and how many sellers achieve it.
key_idea: Add sentinels s_0 = 1-d and s_{m+1} = n+1. Cookies strictly between consecutive eating points a<b are (b-a-1)/d, so total T = m + sum f(s_i, s_{i+1}); removing seller i changes T by f(s_{i-1},s_{i+1}) - f(s_{i-1},s_i) - f(s_i,s_{i+1}) - 1.
solution:
1. Build s with sentinels 1-d and n+1; f(a,b) = (b-a-1)/d.
2. T = m + sum over i=0..m of f(s_i, s_{i+1}).
3. For each real seller i: val = T - f(s_{i-1},s_i) - f(s_i,s_{i+1}) - 1 + f(s_{i-1},s_{i+1}).
4. Track minimum and count. Use long long.

brief: Alice and Bob alternately remove one integer from a sequence (n <= 100), Alice first. Alice wins if the sum of the numbers she took is even. Who wins with optimal play?
key_idea: Only parities matter: state (odd count, even count, parity of Alice's sum, whose turn). Memoized win/lose DP of size 101*101*2*2.
solution:
1. Count o = #odd, e = #even.
2. A(o,e,s): Alice to move. If o=e=0 return s==0. Win if (o>0 and B(o-1,e,s^1)) or (e>0 and B(o,e-1,s)).
3. B(o,e,s): Bob to move. If o=e=0 return s==0. Alice wins only if every Bob move leads to an Alice win: (o==0 or A(o-1,e,s)) and (e==0 or A(o,e-1,s)).
4. Print Alice if A(o,e,0) else Bob.
dry_run:
Sample 1 2 3 4: o=2, e=2.
Whatever Alice takes, Bob can mirror so Alice ends with exactly one odd.
DP gives A(2,2,0) = false -> Bob.
Sample 1 3 5: o=3 -> Alice (takes 2 odds total).

brief: Given a string (length <= 1e5), count strictly increasing sequences of positions of 'a' such that between every two consecutive chosen positions there is at least one 'b'. Mod 1e9+7, non-empty sequences only.
key_idea: Split the string by 'b' into groups; from each group choose at most one 'a' (c_j + 1 ways). Answer = prod (c_j + 1) - 1.
solution:
1. Walk the string keeping cnt = number of 'a' in the current group.
2. On 'b': ans *= (cnt+1), cnt = 0.
3. Other letters are ignored (they don't separate).
4. After the loop ans *= (cnt+1); print ans - 1 mod p.
dry_run:
Sample abbaa: groups 'a' | '' | 'aa' -> counts 1, 0, 2.
(1+1)*(0+1)*(2+1) = 6.
6 - 1 = 5 (expected 5).

brief: Flowers a_1..a_n; collect m flowers left to right where the i-th collected has beauty >= b_i. You may insert at most one flower of any beauty k anywhere. Output the minimum k (0 if no insertion needed, -1 if impossible).
key_idea: Greedy prefix match L[j] = earliest end index after matching b_0..b_{j-1}, greedy suffix match R[j] = latest start index for matching b_j..b_{m-1}. Inserting a flower for b_j works iff L[j] <= R[j+1]; answer = min such b_j.
solution:
1. L[0]=0; greedily scan a matching b in order: L[j+1] = index after the match of b_j (INF if not matched).
2. If L[m] <= n (all matched) print 0.
3. R[m] = n; scan from the right matching b backwards: R[j] = index of the match for b_j (or -INF).
4. For each j: if L[j] <= R[j+1] candidate b_j.
5. Print min candidate or -1.
complexity: O(n + m) per test, O(n + m) space

brief: A string t is hidden in s if it occurs as a subsequence whose indices form an arithmetic progression. Find the maximum number of occurrences of any hidden string (|s| <= 1e5).
key_idea: The best hidden string has length 1 or 2 (every longer occurrence contains a distinct 2-letter prefix occurrence), and any 2-letter subsequence is an AP. Count single letters and all ordered pairs.
solution:
1. cnt[c] = occurrences seen so far; pair[x][y] = number of (i<j) with s_i=x, s_j=y.
2. For each char c: for all x: pair[x][c] += cnt[x]; then cnt[c]++.
3. Answer = max(max cnt, max pair). Use long long (up to ~5e9).
dry_run:
Sample aaabb: cnt a=3, b=2.
pair[a][b] = 3*2 = 6, pair[a][a] = 3, pair[b][b] = 1.
Max = 6 (expected 6).

brief: Humanoid with power h, two green serums (x2) and one blue serum (x3). It can absorb an astronaut with power strictly less than its own, gaining floor(a_i/2). Maximize astronauts absorbed.
key_idea: Sort astronauts; always absorb while possible, and use a serum only when stuck. Only the order of serums matters: try the 3 orders GGB, GBG, BGG and take the best.
solution:
1. Sort a ascending.
2. For each order of serums (2,2,3), (2,3,2), (3,2,2): h' = h, i = 0, k = 0.
3. While i < n: if a[i] < h': h' += a[i]/2, i++; else if k < 3: h' *= order[k++]; else break.
4. Answer = max i over orders. Use long long.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space
dry_run:
Sample 1: h=1, sorted 1 2 8 9. Order G,G,B: stuck -> G (2): absorb 1 (2), stuck at 2 -> G (4): absorb 2 (5).
stuck at 8 -> B (15): absorb 8 (19), absorb 9 (23).
All 4 absorbed -> answer 4.

brief: For a given k (<= 1e5) output at most 500 distinct integer points such that exactly k pairs have Euclidean distance equal to Manhattan distance (i.e. share an x or a y coordinate).
key_idea: s points on one horizontal line give s(s-1)/2 pairs. Greedily take the largest s with s(s-1)/2 <= remaining k, put them on a fresh row with globally unique x values; repeat. At most 489 points are ever needed.
solution:
1. rem = k, row = 0, x = 0 (global counter so no two points share an x).
2. While rem > 0: largest s >= 2 with s(s-1)/2 <= rem; output s points (x++, row); rem -= s(s-1)/2; row++.
3. Points on different rows share no y and no x -> no extra pairs.
4. k = 0: print 0 points.
dry_run:
Own example k=5: s=3 (3 pairs) on row 0: (0,0),(1,0),(2,0); rem 2.
s=2 on row 1: (3,1),(4,1); rem 1.
s=2 on row 2: (5,2),(6,2); rem 0. Total 7 points, 3+1+1 = 5 pairs.

brief: A permutation of length n goes through m experiments; experiment (r, p) sorts the prefix of length r with probability p. Output the probability that the permutation ends up sorted.
key_idea: Let pos = last index where a_i != i. The array ends sorted iff at least one experiment with r >= pos succeeds: answer = 1 - prod over those experiments of (1 - p).
solution:
1. Find pos = largest i with a_i != i. If none, answer 1.0 (already sorted).
2. q = 1.
3. For each experiment (r, p): if r >= pos, q *= (1 - p).
4. Answer 1 - q, printed with 6+ decimals.
complexity: O(n + m) per test, O(n) space
dry_run:
Sample 1: a=4 3 2 1 -> pos=4.
Experiments (1,0.3), (3,1) don't cover; (4,0.6) does: q = 0.4.
Answer 1 - 0.4 = 0.600000.

brief: Segment [1,n]: if its length is even split into two halves; if odd add the middle index m to the lucky value and recurse on [l,m-1] and [m+1,r]. Segments shorter than k are not processed. Output the final lucky value (n <= 2e9).
key_idea: Both halves always have the same length, and the right one is the left one shifted by an offset. So g(len) = (sum of midpoints, number of midpoints) for [1,len]; a shifted copy adds offset*count.
solution:
1. g(len): if len < k return (0,0).
2. If len even: (S,c) = g(len/2); return (2S + c*(len/2), 2c).
3. If len odd: m = (len+1)/2; (S,c) = g((len-1)/2); return (m + 2S + c*m, 1 + 2c).
4. Answer = g(n).S. Only one recursive call per level -> O(log n). Use long long.
complexity: O(log n) per test, O(log n) stack

brief: Cinema hall K x K (K odd, <= 99). For each of N requests for M consecutive seats in one row, choose free seats minimizing total distance sum(|x-c| + |y-c|) to the centre c=(K+1)/2, ties by smaller row then smaller start; print the seats or -1, and mark them taken.
key_idea: Brute force all rows and start positions with prefix sums for 'are these M seats free' and for the sum of |y-c|; pick the minimum cost with ordered tie-breaking.
solution:
1. c = (K+1)/2; D[y] = prefix sums of |y - c|.
2. For each request M: for row x = 1..K, build prefix count of taken seats in that row.
3. For start yl = 1..K-M+1: if no taken seat in [yl, yl+M-1], cost = M*|x-c| + D[yl+M-1] - D[yl-1]; keep if strictly smaller (gives tie order).
4. Print best and mark seats taken, else -1.
5. (The remoteness formula is an image on the page; it is the standard Manhattan-to-centre sum, consistent with the samples.)
dry_run:
Sample K=3 (c=2), requests 1 2 3 1: M=1 -> (2,2) cost 0.
M=2: row1 1-2 cost 2+1=3, row1 2-3 cost 3, row2 blocked, row3 3 -> '1 1 2'.
M=3: only row 3 free -> '3 1 3'. M=1: row2 seat1 cost 1 -> '2 1 1'.

brief: Train with n wagons; a controller walks back and forth (reversing at the ends), a stowaway tries to avoid him. Each minute is moving (stowaway moves -1/0/+1 first, then controller) or idle (stowaway leaves, controller moves, stowaway re-enters any wagon). Last minute is terminal. Output 'Stowaway' or 'Controller t' (minute of capture).
key_idea: The controller is deterministic, so track the SET of wagons where the stowaway could still be alive (a reachability DP); he is caught exactly when the set becomes empty.
solution:
1. S = {m}; pos = k; dir = -1 for 'to head', +1 for 'to tail'.
2. Moving minute: S' = {p-1,p,p+1} in range for p in S, minus pos; controller moves (pos += dir; reverse at 1 or n); remove new pos from S'.
3. Idle minute: if it's the last minute -> Stowaway wins. Else controller moves, S = all wagons except pos.
4. If S becomes empty at minute i print 'Controller i'.
5. If the string ends (last char is '1') -> 'Stowaway'.

brief: Array of digits (n <= 1e5). Count subarrays whose sum equals their length.
key_idea: Subtract 1 from every element: a good subarray has sum 0, i.e. two equal prefix sums. Count equal pairs with a hash map.
solution:
1. b_i = a_i - 1; P_0 = 0.
2. cnt[0] = 1; for each i: P += b_i; ans += cnt[P]; cnt[P]++.
3. Use long long for the answer (up to ~5e9).
dry_run:
Sample '120': b = 0, 1, -1; prefixes 0, 0, 1, 0.
Value 0 occurs 3 times -> 3 pairs.
Answer 3 (expected 3).

brief: In an infinite k-ary tree, child edges have weights 1..k. Count root paths with total weight n that use at least one edge of weight >= d, mod 1e9+7 (n, k <= 100).
key_idea: dp[s][f] = number of paths with weight s, f = whether an edge >= d has been used.
solution:
1. dp[0][0] = 1.
2. For s = 1..n, for w = 1..min(k, s): dp[s][1] += dp[s-w][1] + (w >= d ? dp[s-w][0] : 0); dp[s][0] += (w < d ? dp[s-w][0] : 0).
3. Answer dp[n][1] mod p.
4. Equivalent: all paths with weights <= k minus paths with weights <= d-1.
dry_run:
Sample n=3,k=3,d=2: paths of weight 3: 1+1+1, 1+2, 2+1, 3.
Those with an edge >= 2: 1+2, 2+1, 3.
dp[3][1] = 3 (expected 3).

brief: Tree rooted at city 1 (n <= 2e5). Choose exactly k industry cities; each industry city's envoy gains happiness equal to the number of tourism cities on its path to the root. Maximize the total.
key_idea: Optimal choices are closed downward (children before parents), so choosing v contributes depth(v) - (subtree_size(v) - 1). Take the k largest such values.
solution:
1. BFS/DFS from 1 to get depth (root depth 0) and an order; accumulate subtree sizes in reverse order.
2. val(v) = depth(v) - (size(v) - 1).
3. Sort values descending, sum the top k (long long).
4. Picking v adds its depth but each of its size-1 descendants (already industry) loses 1.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

brief: Start at index 1 with score a_1; make exactly k moves, each right (+a_{x+1}) or left (+a_{x-1}), with at most z left moves and never two lefts in a row. Maximize the score (z <= 5).
key_idea: Fix the number of left moves t <= z. The final position is p = k - 2t; spend all left moves oscillating on the best adjacent pair (i, i+1) with i <= p.
solution:
1. For t = 0..z: p = k - 2t (0-indexed); stop if p < 0.
2. score = (a_0 + ... + a_p) + t * max_{i <= p, i+1 < n} (a_i + a_{i+1}).
3. Track the running prefix sum and the running max pair.
4. Answer = max over t.
complexity: O(n * z) per test, O(n) space

brief: n strings must end in lexicographic order (in the given positions); reversing string i costs c_i. Find the minimum total cost or -1.
key_idea: dp[i][0/1] = min cost with string i kept / reversed and strings 1..i sorted; transitions compare the 2 versions of string i-1 with the 2 versions of string i.
solution:
1. s[i][0] = original, s[i][1] = reversed.
2. dp[0][0] = 0, dp[0][1] = c_0.
3. dp[i][b] = min over a with s[i-1][a] <= s[i][b] of dp[i-1][a], plus (b ? c_i : 0).
4. INF if no valid a. Answer min(dp[n-1][0], dp[n-1][1]) or -1. Use long long.
complexity: O(total length) time, O(total length) space
dry_run:
Sample 1: 'ba','ac', costs 1,2: dp0 = {0, 1} ('ba' / 'ab').
string 'ac': 'ba' <= 'ac'? no; 'ab' <= 'ac' yes -> dp1[0] = 1.
'ca': both fine -> dp1[1] = 0 + 2 = 2. Answer 1.

brief: Tree with n vertices; vertex v must get a value a_v in [l_v, r_v]. Maximize the sum over edges of |a_u - a_v|.
key_idea: An optimal assignment uses only endpoints l_v or r_v. dp[v][0/1] = best subtree value when v takes l_v / r_v.
solution:
1. Root at 1; get BFS order and parents.
2. In reverse order: for each child c of v and x in {0,1} (val = l_v or r_v): dp[v][x] += max(dp[c][0] + |val - l_c|, dp[c][1] + |val - r_c|).
3. Answer max(dp[1][0], dp[1][1]). Use long long.
4. Endpoint argument: |a - x| summed over neighbours is convex in a, so the max is at an endpoint.

brief: Array starts all 1s. One operation: choose i and x >= 1 and add floor(a_i/x) to a_i. With at most k operations, you earn c_i for each i with a_i = b_i (b_i <= 1000). Maximize coins.
key_idea: Precompute steps[v] = min operations to reach v from 1 (BFS over values <= 1000, at most 12). Then it's a 0/1 knapsack with weight steps[b_i], value c_i, capacity min(k, 12n).
solution:
1. BFS/DP: steps[1] = 0; for v, for x = 1..v: w = v + v/x, if w <= 1000 steps[w] = min(steps[w], steps[v]+1).
2. cap = min(k, sum of steps[b_i]) (capacity beyond that is useless).
3. 0/1 knapsack: for each i, for j = cap..w_i: dp[j] = max(dp[j], dp[j-w_i] + c_i).
4. Answer dp[cap].
complexity: O(1000^2) precompute + O(n * 12n) knapsack, O(12n) space
dry_run:
Sample 1: b = 1 7 5 2, c = 2 6 5 2, k=4. steps: 1->0, 2->1, 5->3 (1,2,4,5), 7->4 (1,2,3,6,7).
Weights 0,4,3,1; capacity 4.
Best: items b=1 (2) + b=5 (5) + b=2 (2) = weight 4, value 9.
Answer 9 (expected 9).

brief: Array a (n <= 1000). Operation: choose i < n with a_i <= a_{i+1} and increase a_i by 1. With at most k operations maximize max(a).
key_idea: Fix the index i that becomes the maximum X. It needs a_{i+1} >= X-1, a_{i+2} >= X-2, ... until some original a_{i+j} >= X-j already; cost = sum of (X-j - a_{i+j}) over the raised ones. Feasibility is monotone in X: binary search per i.
solution:
1. For each i: binary search X in [a_i, a_i + k].
2. check(i, X): cost = 0; for j = 0..: if i+j == n -> infeasible; need = X - j; if a[i+j] >= need -> feasible if cost <= k; else cost += need - a[i+j].
3. Track the best feasible X over all i (also the original max).
4. Use long long for costs.
complexity: O(n^2 log k) time, O(n) space
dry_run:
Sample 1 3 3, k=4: i=1 (value 3): X=4 needs a3 >= 3 -> yes, cost 1.
X=5 needs a3 >= 4 (cost 1+1) then index past end -> infeasible.
i=0: X=4 needs a1>=3 ok, cost 3 <= 4 -> 4. Answer 4.

brief: A sequence a was cut into segments and each segment's length was written immediately to its left or right, giving b. Given b, decide if this is possible.
key_idea: dp[i] = prefix of length i can be fully explained. Element at position i (1-indexed) with value v either is a left marker covering i+1..i+v (dp[i+v] |= dp[i-1]) or a right marker covering i-v..i-1 (dp[i] |= dp[i-v-1]).
solution:
1. dp[0] = true.
2. For i = 1..n, v = b_i:
   a) if i - v - 1 >= 0 and dp[i-v-1]: dp[i] = true (right marker).
   b) if dp[i-1] and i + v <= n: dp[i+v] = true (left marker).
3. Process i increasing (both updates only depend on smaller indices being final).
4. YES iff dp[n].
dry_run:
Sample [3,1]: i=1 v=3: left marker needs 1+3<=2 no; right needs i-v-1<0.
i=2 v=1: right: dp[0] -> dp[2] = true (segment [3] with length 1 to its right).
YES (expected YES). Sample [1] -> NO.

brief: Array a (0-indexed). Reverse at most one subarray to maximize the sum of elements at even indices.
key_idea: Only even-length reversals change the sum; they swap parities of pairs. Gain arrays: g1 = a[i+1]-a[i] for even i, g2 = a[i]-a[i+1] for odd i; answer = base + max(0, best Kadane subarray of g1 or g2).
solution:
1. base = sum of a[i] for even i.
2. g1: for i = 0,2,4,...: a[i+1] - a[i]. g2: for i = 1,3,...: a[i] - a[i+1].
3. Kadane max subarray sum on each (allow empty -> 0).
4. Answer base + max gain. Use long long.

brief: Arrays a, b of length n (<= 5000). Reverse at most one subarray of a to maximize sum a_i * b_i.
key_idea: Expand around every center: reversing [l, r] from [l+1, r-1] adds a_l*b_r + a_r*b_l - a_l*b_l - a_r*b_r to the gain. O(n^2) total.
solution:
1. base = sum a_i*b_i.
2. For each center c, for both odd (l=r=c) and even (l=c, r=c+1) centers: gain = 0.
3. While l >= 0 and r < n: gain += a[l]*b[r] + a[r]*b[l] - a[l]*b[l] - a[r]*b[r] (for l == r this is 0); best = max(best, gain); l--, r++.
4. Answer base + best (best >= 0). Use long long.
dry_run:
Sample 2: a=13 37, b=2 4: base = 26 + 148 = 174.
Reverse [0,1]: 37*2 + 13*4 = 126 < 174 -> gain negative.
Answer 174 (expected 174).

brief: From string s (n <= 5000) you may delete the last character or double the string (s = s+s) any number of times. Output the lexicographically smallest string of length exactly k (k <= 5000).
key_idea: Every reachable result is some prefix of s repeated infinitely and cut to length k. Try all n prefixes and take the minimum.
solution:
1. For p = 1..n: build t of length k with t[i] = s[i % p].
2. Keep the lexicographically smallest t.
3. Print it.
4. (Hard version uses a linear greedy; easy version O(n*k) is fine.)
dry_run:
Sample 'abcd', k=5: p=1 -> 'aaaaa'; p=2 -> 'ababa'; p=3 -> 'abcab'...
Minimum is 'aaaaa'.
Output aaaaa (expected).

brief: Each operation replaces every digit d of n by the decimal form of d+1 (9 -> 10). After m operations (m <= 2e5, t <= 2e5 queries), output the length of the number mod 1e9+7.
key_idea: Digits evolve independently. L[x] = length obtained from digit 0 after x operations: L[x] = 1 for x < 10, else L[x-9] + L[x-10] (0 becomes 10 after 10 steps: a '1' (= '0' one step ahead) and a '0'). Digit d after m ops has length L[m+d].
solution:
1. Precompute L[0..2e5+10]: L[x] = 1 for x < 10; L[x] = (L[x-9] + L[x-10]) mod p.
2. For each query read n as a string and m.
3. Answer = sum over digits d of L[m + d] mod p.
complexity: O(M + total digits) time, O(M) space

brief: Cans labeled 1, 2, 3, ... are stacked in a triangular pyramid (row r has r cans). Hitting the can labeled n^2 knocks it and every can resting above it; output the sum of squares of labels that fall (n <= 1e6).
key_idea: Can (r,c) is supported by (r-1,c-1) and (r-1,c). Sum over the 'cone' above via inclusion-exclusion: S[r][c] = v^2 + S[r-1][c-1] + S[r-1][c] - S[r-2][c-1].
solution:
1. Lay labels row by row: row r holds labels r(r-1)/2+1 .. r(r+1)/2, positions c = 1..r.
2. S[r][c] = label^2 + S[r-1][c-1] + S[r-1][c] - S[r-2][c-1] (out-of-range = 0).
3. Store ans[label] = S[r][c]; precompute until label 1e6 is covered (~1415 rows).
4. Answer each query by lookup (unsigned/long long).
complexity: O(N) precompute (N ≈ 1e6 cans), O(1) per query

brief: A string over {a,b,c} is beautiful if it has no palindromic substring of length >= 2. For m queries (l, r) output the minimum number of changes to make s[l..r] beautiful (n, m <= 2e5).
key_idea: A beautiful string must have s_i != s_{i+1} and s_i != s_{i+2}, so it is periodic with period 3 following one of the 6 permutations of 'abc'. Precompute prefix mismatch counts for each of the 6 patterns.
solution:
1. For each permutation p of "abc" (6 total): pre[p][i+1] = pre[p][i] + (s[i] != p[i % 3]).
2. Query (l, r): answer = min over p of pre[p][r] - pre[p][l-1].
3. The pattern is anchored at absolute index i, which is fine since all 6 shifts/permutations are covered.
dry_run:
Sample s=baacb, query (1,3) 'baa': pattern 'bac' (perm b,a,c) mismatches 1.
query (2,3) 'aa': best pattern costs 1.
query (4,5) 'cb': some pattern matches exactly -> 0.

brief: Permutation p of length n (sum n <= 5000). For each i choose a_i = p_i or a_i = 2n - p_i. Minimize the number of inversions of a.
key_idea: For a pair of values x < y, only the smaller value's choice matters: keeping x makes it an inversion iff y is before x; mirroring x makes it an inversion iff y is after x. So each element independently picks min(#larger before, #larger after).
solution:
1. For each i: before = #j < i with p_j > p_i, after = #j > i with p_j > p_i.
2. Answer = sum of min(before, after).
3. O(n^2) is fine (sum n <= 5000); a BIT gives O(n log n).
dry_run:
Sample 2 1 3: element 1: larger before = 1 (2), after = 1 (3) -> 1.
element 2: before 0 -> 0. element 3: 0.
Total 1 (expected 1).

brief: Count pairs of arrays (a, b) of length m (m <= 10) with values in 1..n (n <= 1000), a non-decreasing, b non-increasing, and a_i <= b_i, modulo 1e9+7.
key_idea: a_1 <= ... <= a_m <= b_m <= ... <= b_1, so the sequence a followed by reversed b is any non-decreasing sequence of length 2m over 1..n: answer = C(n + 2m - 1, 2m).
solution:
1. Only the condition a_m <= b_m matters once a is non-decreasing and b non-increasing.
2. Count non-decreasing sequences of length L = 2m over n values: stars and bars C(n+L-1, L).
3. Compute with factorials and modular inverse (or Pascal's triangle up to 1020).
4. Alternative DP: dp[len][last] with prefix sums.
complexity: O(n + m) time, O(n + m) space
dry_run:
Sample n=2,m=2: C(2+4-1, 4) = C(5,4) = 5.
Sample n=10,m=1: C(11,2) = 55.
Both match.

brief: Tree with n vertices. Remove exactly two vertices (with their edges). Maximize the number of connected components left.
key_idea: Removing u then v gives deg(u) + deg(v) - 1 components, minus 1 more if u and v are adjacent. Try every u as the first vertex and pick the best v from a multiset of degrees after decrementing u's neighbours.
solution:
1. Compute degrees; put all degrees in a multiset.
2. For each u: erase deg(u); for each neighbour w, replace deg(w) by deg(w)-1 in the multiset.
3. cand = deg(u) + (max in multiset) - 1; answer = max.
4. Restore the multiset. Total O(n log n).
5. n = 2 gives 0 automatically (deg 1 + deg 0 - 1).
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run:
Sample 3: edges 1-2,1-3,2-4,4-5,5-6,5-7. deg: 1:2, 2:2, 3:1, 4:2, 5:3, 6:1, 7:1.
u=5: neighbours 4,6,7 decrement -> max remaining deg = 2 (vertex 1 or 2).
3 + 2 - 1 = 4 (expected 4).

brief: Arrays a (n) and b (m), values < 512. For each a_i pick any b_j and set c_i = a_i & b_j. Minimize c_1 | c_2 | ... | c_n.
key_idea: The answer is < 512, so try every candidate A from 0 upward: A is achievable iff every a_i has some b_j with (a_i & b_j) a submask of A.
solution:
1. For A = 0..511:
2. ok = for all i exists j with ((a_i & b_j) | A) == A.
3. Print the first ok A (the OR of such choices is a submask of A, and minimality makes it exactly A).
complexity: O(512 * n * m) ≈ 2e7 time, O(1) extra space
dry_run:
Sample 1: a = 2 6 4 0, b = 2 4. A=0: a=2 needs 2&b = 0 -> b=4 ok; a=6: 6&2=2, 6&4=4 -> fail.
A=1 fails similarly; A=2: a=6 & 2 = 2 submask of 2 ok; a=4 & 2 = 0 ok.
Answer 2.

brief: Tree with n vertices. Remove exactly k edges so every component has at least x vertices; find the maximum x.
key_idea: For a fixed x, greedily cut a subtree as soon as its accumulated size reaches x (bottom-up); feasible iff at least k+1 pieces of size >= x are formed (extra cuts can be merged back). Binary search x.
solution:
1. Root at 1, compute a BFS order and parents.
2. check(x): rem[v] = 1; process vertices in reverse order: add rem[v] to parent unless rem[v] >= x for a non-root v (then cnt++ and pass 0).
3. At the root: if rem[root] >= x then cnt++.
4. Feasible iff cnt >= k+1.
5. Binary search the largest x in [1, n/(k+1)].
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run:
Own example: chain 1-2-3-4, k=1. x=2: node4 rem 1, node3 rem 2 -> cut (cnt 1), node2 rem 1, root rem 2 -> cnt 2 >= 2 ok.
x=3: node2 gets 3 -> cnt 1, root rem 1 < 3 -> cnt 1 < 2 fail.
Answer 2.

brief: Given a < b (<= 1e6). Operations: a += 1, b += 1, or a = a | b. Find the minimum number of operations to make a equal b.
key_idea: Optimal plans: just increment a (b - a ops), or increment a to a', increment b to b', then one OR (needs a' submask of b', result b'). Enumerate a' in [a, b) and build the smallest b' >= b with a' ⊆ b' bit by bit.
solution:
1. ans = b - a.
2. For each a' in [a, b): build b' from high bit to low: copy b's bit when it is 1; at the first bit where b has 0 but a' has 1, set it and stop (lower bits become 0).
3. Final value is a' | b'; cost = (a' - a) + ((a' | b') - b) + 1.
4. ans = min over a'. Sum of b <= 1e6 keeps it fast.
complexity: O(b log b) per test, O(1) space
dry_run:
Sample a=2, b=5: a'=2: b has bit1=0, a' has bit1=1 -> b' = 100|010 = 6; a'|b' = 6: cost 0 + 1 + 1 = 2.
ans = min(3, 2, ...) = 2 (expected 2).
Sample 1 3: a'=1 ⊆ 3: cost 0+0+1 = 1.

brief: Binary tree rooted at 1 (root infected). Each round you may delete one non-infected vertex, then infection spreads to neighbours. Maximize the number of vertices saved (deleted vertices don't count).
key_idea: When v gets infected you delete one of its children; that child's subtree minus itself (size-1) is saved, and infection continues into the other child. dp[v] = max(sz[c1]-1 + dp[c2], sz[c2]-1 + dp[c1]).
solution:
1. Root at 1, compute subtree sizes and children (iterative order).
2. Leaf: dp = 0. One child c: dp = sz[c] - 1.
3. Two children: dp = max(sz[c1]-1 + dp[c2], sz[c2]-1 + dp[c1]).
4. Answer dp[1].
dry_run:
Own example: edges 1-2, 1-3, 3-4, 3-5 (sizes: 2:1, 3:3).
dp[3] = max(0 + 0, 0 + 0) = 0; dp[2] = 0.
dp[1] = max(sz2-1 + dp3, sz3-1 + dp2) = max(0, 2) = 2 (delete 3, save 4 and 5).

brief: Given positive x, y (<= 1e9), find k >= 0 (k <= 1e18) with (x+k) + (y+k) = (x+k) XOR (y+k), or print -1.
key_idea: Sum equals XOR iff the two numbers share no set bit. If x == y it's impossible. Otherwise push the larger one up to a power of two 2^p >= max: k = 2^p - max; the smaller becomes min + k < 2^p, so no common bits.
solution:
1. If x == y print -1.
2. p = smallest power of two with 2^p >= max(x, y).
3. k = 2^p - max(x, y). Then max+k = 2^p (single bit) and min+k < 2^p.
4. Print k (any valid answer is accepted).
complexity: O(log max) per test, O(1) space
dry_run:
Sample 19 10: max 19 -> 2^5 = 32, k = 13: 32 and 23 share no bits (sum 55 = xor 55).
Sample prints 1 (also valid); any answer accepted.
Sample 6 6 -> -1.

brief: Binary string s (length <= 1e6) and k (<= 1e6). Count substrings containing exactly k ones.
key_idea: With prefix count P of ones, a substring (l, r] has P_r - P_l = k; count earlier prefixes with value P_r - k using a frequency array.
solution:
1. cnt array of size n+1, cnt[0] = 1, P = 0.
2. For each char: P += (c == '1'); if P >= k ans += cnt[P - k]; cnt[P]++.
3. Use long long for the answer (up to ~5e11).
4. k = 0 is handled naturally.

brief: Mushrooms with toxicity a_i and limit x. Eating a segment left to right, g += a_i and if g > x then g resets to 0. Count segments [l, r] whose final g is nonzero.
key_idea: From l, let r be the first index where sum(l..r) > x: segments ending before r are good (r - l of them), at r g resets to 0 and the process restarts at r+1, so dp[l] = (r - l) + dp[r+1].
solution:
1. Prefix sums P (long long).
2. For l = n-1 down to 0: r = first index with P[r+1] - P[l] > x (upper_bound on P).
3. If none: dp[l] = n - l; else dp[l] = (r - l) + dp[r+1] (dp[n] = 0).
4. Answer = sum of dp[l].
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run:
Sample 1 1 1 1, x=2: dp[3]=1; dp[2]: no reset -> 2.
dp[1]: sum exceeds at r=3 -> 2 + dp[4]=0 -> 2; dp[0]: r=2 -> 2 + dp[3] = 3.
Total 1+2+2+3 = 8 (expected 8).

brief: Build t starting from empty z; one operation appends any subsequence of s. Find the minimum number of operations, or -1 if some letter of t is missing from s.
key_idea: Greedy: match t through s as far as possible, then start a new pass. Precompute nxt[i][c] = first position >= i holding c to make each step O(1).
solution:
1. nxt[n][c] = -1; for i = n-1..0: nxt[i] = nxt[i+1], nxt[i][s[i]] = i.
2. ops = 1, pos = 0. For each char c of t: if nxt[0][c] == -1 -> answer -1.
3. If pos == n or nxt[pos][c] == -1: ops++, pos = 0.
4. pos = nxt[pos][c] + 1.
5. Print ops.
dry_run:
Sample s=ty, t=yyt: y at 1 -> pos 2; y: none after -> ops 2, y at 1 -> pos 2.
t: none after -> ops 3, t at 0.
Answer 3 (expected 3).

brief: n rectangles (h, w <= 1000). Each query (hs, ws, hb, wb) asks for the total area of rectangles with hs < h < hb and ws < w < wb.
key_idea: Coordinates are at most 1000, so accumulate areas into a 1001x1001 grid indexed by (h, w) and answer each query with a 2D prefix-sum rectangle query on [hs+1, hb-1] x [ws+1, wb-1].
solution:
1. g[h][w] += h*w for each rectangle.
2. Build 2D prefix sums S (long long).
3. Query: rows hs+1..hb-1, cols ws+1..wb-1: S[hb-1][wb-1] - S[hs][wb-1] - S[hb-1][ws] + S[hs][ws].
4. Reset the grid per test case (t <= 100, 1e6 cells each is fine).
complexity: O(1000^2 + n + q) per test, O(1000^2) space
dry_run:
Sample 1: rectangles 2x3 (area 6) and 3x2 (area 6); query 1 1 3 4.
Heights 2..2, widths 2..3: only (2,3) inside -> 6.
(3,2) excluded because h=3 is not < 3. Output 6.

brief: Given a sequence (n <= 1e5), find the longest contiguous subsegment that can be made strictly increasing by changing at most one element.
key_idea: L[i] = increasing run ending at i, R[i] = increasing run starting at i. Changing a[i] joins L[i-1] and R[i+1] when a[i+1] - a[i-1] >= 2; otherwise you can still extend one side by 1.
solution:
1. Compute L and R (strictly increasing runs).
2. ans = max over i of L[i-1] + 1 and R[i+1] + 1 (change a[i] to extend one run), capped by n.
3. If 0 < i < n-1 and a[i+1] - a[i-1] >= 2: ans = max(ans, L[i-1] + 1 + R[i+1]).
4. n = 1 -> 1.

brief: Score = number of prefixes with sum 0. You may replace any element equal to 0 with any integer (each zero once). Maximize the score.
key_idea: Each zero controls the segment from it up to the next zero: changing it shifts all those prefix sums by the same amount, so pick the shift that makes the most frequent prefix sum in that segment become 0.
solution:
1. Before the first zero: count prefixes with sum 0 as-is.
2. For each zero at position z, consider prefix sums P_z..P_{next zero - 1} (original values).
3. Add the maximum frequency among those sums (setting a_z = -mostFrequent).
4. Sum up; use long long sums and a map per segment.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run:
Sample 2 0 1 -1 0: prefix 2 | zero at 1: segment sums 2, 3, 2 -> max freq 2 (value 2).
Zero at 4: segment sums 2 -> freq 1.
Total 0 + 2 + 1 = 3 (expected 3).

brief: Sequence a and number x (all <= 500). Operation: choose i with a_i > x and swap a_i with x. Find the minimum operations to make a non-decreasing, or -1.
key_idea: Scan left to right: stop as soon as the array is sorted; otherwise any a_i > x must be swapped now (later swaps only increase x, so skipping it would leave a too-large early element).
solution:
1. For i = 0..n-1: if a is already sorted, break.
2. If a[i] > x: swap(a[i], x), ops++.
3. After the loop, if a is sorted print ops, else -1.
4. Checking sortedness each step is O(n), total O(n^2) with n <= 500.

brief: Alice adds numbers but carries to the column two places left instead of one. Given n (<= 1e9), count ordered pairs of positive integers (a, b) whose Alice-sum is n.
key_idea: Carries from odd columns only affect odd columns and likewise for even ones, so split n's digits by alternating positions into two normal numbers A and B. Pairs = (A+1)(B+1), minus 2 for the pairs where a or b is 0.
solution:
1. Read n as a string; build A from digits at even indices and B from digits at odd indices (both left to right).
2. Each is an ordinary addition: A has A+1 ordered splits, B has B+1.
3. Answer = (A+1)*(B+1) - 2 (exclude a=0 and b=0).
4. Use long long.

brief: n x m matrix (values <= 1023). Pick one entry per row so the XOR is > 0; print TAK and the chosen columns, or NIE.
key_idea: Take column 1 in every row. If the XOR is already nonzero, done. Otherwise changing a single row to any entry different from its first entry makes the XOR nonzero; if no such entry exists, answer NIE.
solution:
1. X = XOR of a[i][0] over all rows; choice = all 1s.
2. If X != 0 print TAK and choices.
3. Else find any (i, j) with a[i][j] != a[i][0]; set choice[i] = j+1 (new XOR = a[i][0] ^ a[i][j] != 0).
4. If none exists print NIE.
dry_run:
Sample 2: rows [7,7,7], [7,7,10]: X = 7^7 = 0.
Row 2 col 3 has 10 != 7 -> choose it: 7 ^ 10 = 13 > 0.
Output TAK / 1 3. Sample 1 (all zeros) -> NIE.

brief: Open n chests in order. A good key costs k; a bad key is free but halves (floor) the coins in this and every later chest. Maximize final coins.
key_idea: It's optimal to use good keys first and then only bad keys (swapping a bad key before a good key never hurts). After ~31 halvings everything is 0, so for each split i compute the tail in O(31).
solution:
1. Prefix sums P of a.
2. For i = 0..n (good keys on the first i chests): val = P[i] - i*k.
3. Tail: for j = i..min(n-1, i+31): val += a[j] >> (j - i + 1).
4. Answer = max val (long long; can be negative contributions from k, but i=0 gives >= 0).

brief: Permutation p with max(p_i, p_{i+1}) > p_{i+2} for all i (n <= 5e5). Output the sum, over all subarrays, of the length of the longest decreasing subsequence.
key_idea: Under the condition, LDS of a subarray = its length minus the number of ascents (p_i < p_{i+1}) inside it. So answer = sum of all subarray lengths - sum over ascents at i of i*(n-i) (subarrays containing both i and i+1).
solution:
1. total = sum over lengths: sum_{i=1..n} i*(n-i+1).
2. For each i (1-indexed) with p_i < p_{i+1}: total -= i*(n-i).
3. Print total (long long; ~2e16).
4. Why: greedily take every element except the smaller one of each ascent; the condition guarantees the rest is decreasing.

brief: n planes in a row and a particle with decay age k. Each plane lets a particle pass and also emits a copy in the opposite direction with age k-1 (age 1 makes no copies). Count all particles produced, mod 1e9+7.
key_idea: dp[k][x] = particles generated by one particle of age k with x planes ahead (so n-x behind). Crossing the j-th plane ahead emits an age k-1 particle with (n-x)+(j-1) planes ahead of it: dp[k][x] = 1 + sum_{y=n-x}^{n-1} dp[k-1][y].
solution:
1. dp[1][x] = 1 for all x; dp[k][0] = 1.
2. For age a = 2..k: prefix sums of dp[a-1]; dp[a][x] = 1 + (pre[n] - pre[n-x]).
3. Answer dp[k][n].
4. Keep only two rows; per test O(n*k), sums bounded by 1000.

brief: n+m+1 candidates arrive in order; each goes to programmer (if a_i > b_i) or tester role, or the other role if that one is full (n programmers, m testers). For each candidate, output the team skill if that candidate does not come.
key_idea: Simulate the first n+m candidates (that's the answer when the last one is absent). Removing candidate i frees its role r: the first later candidate j who preferred r but was pushed to the other role now takes r, and the last candidate fills the freed other slot; if no such j, the last candidate takes r.
solution:
1. Simulate candidates 1..n+m greedily: role[i], base = total skill. val(i, r) = a_i or b_i.
2. Precompute nxt[r][i] = first j > i (j <= n+m) with preferred role r but assigned the other role.
3. For i <= n+m with role r: if j = nxt[r][i] exists: ans = base - val(i,r) + val(j,r) - val(j,!r) + val(last,!r); else ans = base - val(i,r) + val(last,r).
4. For the last candidate: ans = base.
5. Use long long.
complexity: O(n + m) per test, O(n + m) space
dry_run:
Sample n=1,m=0: a = 2 1, b = 1 2. First candidate: programmer (2), base = 2.
Remove 1: no later j; last candidate takes programmer: 2 - 2 + 1 = 1.
Remove 2 (last): 2. Output '1 2' (expected).
